title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed research shows U.S. domestic equity funds carry large hidden U.S.-China geoeconomic exposure via supply chains (20.3% of assets; 43.3% for tech funds). Export controls on Chinese customers knock -3.6% off U.S. suppliers, drive persistent active selling, hit passive funds harder, and exposed stocks earn ~1%/month risk premium.

themes.theme: Hidden China exposure in domestic equity funds

insights.claim: U.S. domestic equity mutual funds invest on average 20.3% of assets in U.S. firms that have at least one Chinese customer, meaning 'domestic' portfolios carry substantial U.S.-China geoeconomic exposure.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: A 'U.S.-only' equity allocation is not insulated from U.S.-China policy shocks.
insights.quote: On average, 20.3 percent of fund assets are invested in U.S. firms with at least one Chinese customer.

insights.claim: Science and technology mutual funds invest 43.3% of their portfolios in U.S. firms connected to Chinese customers, the highest exposure among styles, with growth and tech styles generally most exposed.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Tech/growth style allocations are the main carriers of export-control risk in domestic portfolios.
insights.quote: invest 43.3 percent of their portfolios in domestic firms

insights.claim: Within China-connected holdings of domestic equity funds, U.S. suppliers to Chinese customers newly targeted by export controls account for 8.4% of assets.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: A meaningful slice of China-linked holdings is directly in the firing line of new BIS entity listings.

insights.claim: Geoeconomic shocks are hard to diversify away within domestic stocks because a single policy action can hit many U.S. firms through a common foreign customer or supply-chain exposure.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Count of holdings is a poor diversification metric; map shared foreign revenue/customer exposures instead.
insights.quote: Geoeconomic shocks are therefore difficult to diversify away because they can affect multiple domestic stocks through a common foreign exposure.

insights.claim: Investors should assess not only where a stock is listed but where the firm earns its revenue and how exposed those relationships are to geopolitical policy shocks, as economic policy becomes increasingly tied to national security.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Revenue-geography and customer mapping become core risk-management inputs.

themes.theme: Export controls as a supplier-stock shock

insights.claim: U.S. suppliers suffer a cumulative abnormal stock return of about -3.6% after their Chinese customers are added to a U.S. export-control list, with most of the decline occurring in the first five trading days.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: New BIS entity-list additions are a tradable negative catalyst for the targeted firms' U.S. suppliers, front-loaded within a week.

insights.claim: Since 2014, U.S. export controls from the Bureau of Industry and Security have been used frequently in the U.S.-China tech rivalry, especially in semiconductors, telecommunications, artificial intelligence and advanced computing.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Semis, telecom, AI and compute suppliers are the sectors most exposed to recurring entity-list risk.

insights.claim: Conditional on an export-control event, a one-standard-deviation (2.5%) increase in a fund's exposure to affected U.S. suppliers is associated with a 22 basis-point decline in monthly returns, along with higher volatility.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Fund-level performance drag from export controls is measurable and material relative to typical active alpha.
insights.quote: a one standard deviation increase in exposure (2.5 percent) is associated with a 22-basis-point decline in monthly returns

insights.claim: Active fund managers sell not only U.S. suppliers directly affected by new export controls but also other China-linked U.S. firms not affected by the current announcement, and selling of affected suppliers persists three months later.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Export-control announcements trigger contagion selling across China-linked names and multi-month flow pressure, not a one-day blip.

insights.claim: Export controls act as a wake-up call: persistent and broad selling suggests investors learn that geoeconomic risk was embedded in supply-chain links that were not fully priced or understood beforehand.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Each new control round can reprice the whole China-linked cohort as investors update on hidden exposure.
insights.quote: export controls might serve as a wake-up call

insights.claim: Passive funds suffer more from export-control shocks than active funds: a one-standard-deviation exposure increase cuts passive monthly returns by 31 bp versus 22 bp for active, and passive funds see next-month outflows of about 0.35% of assets while active outflows are insignificant.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Index trackers absorb the full geoeconomic hit; active rebalancing provides partial insulation.
insights.quote: passive funds experience a 31-basis-point decline in monthly returns, compared with 22 basis points for active funds

insights.claim: Exposed active funds respond to export-control performance shortfalls by holding more concentrated portfolios and tilting toward lottery-like stocks, apparently taking extra risk to limit future outflows.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Watch for risk-shifting in active funds after geoeconomic hits; it may raise demand for high-volatility names and fund tail risk.

insights.claim: Specialist managers and higher-fee funds experience smaller performance declines after export-control shocks, while traditional market-timing and stock-picking skills do not predict better outcomes.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Geoeconomic risk management is a distinct skill: mapping policy shocks onto firms' positions in global value chains, not generic stock-picking.
insights.quote: traditional market-timing and stock-picking skills do not predict better outcomes

insights.claim: A long-short portfolio buying U.S. firms previously exposed to export controls and shorting unexposed firms earns about 1% per month in abnormal returns after standard risk-factor adjustment, indicating geoeconomic exposure is a priced risk factor.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Export-control-exposed U.S. suppliers may offer a compensated risk premium for investors able to bear policy-shock risk.

insights.claim: The market treats geoeconomic exposure not as a one-time news event but as a persistent priced risk for which investors demand compensation.
insights.speaker: Matteo Crosignani
insights.so_what: Post-shock drawdowns in exposed suppliers are partly compensation for ongoing risk rather than pure mispricing.
insights.quote: as a priced risk for which investors demand compensation
